question: Air brakes are actually made up of three different braking systems. What are they?
choice_a: Primary, secondary, and tertiary brake
choice_b: Front brake, rear brake, and trailer brake
choice_c: Service brake, parking brake, and emergency brake
choice_d: Foot brake, hand brake, and engine brake
explanation: Air brakes are really three different braking systems: the service brake, the parking brake, and the emergency brake.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Introduction

question: What does the emergency brake system in an air brake setup use to stop the vehicle during a brake system failure?
choice_a: A secondary fuel shutoff
choice_b: The transmission alone
choice_c: Parts of the service and parking brake systems
choice_d: A completely separate hydraulic system
explanation: The emergency brake system uses parts of the service and parking brake systems to stop the vehicle in the event of a brake system failure.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Introduction

question: How is the air compressor typically connected to the engine?
choice_a: Through a hydraulic pump
choice_b: Through the transmission's power take-off only
choice_c: Through gears or a v-belt
choice_d: It is not connected to the engine at all
explanation: The air compressor pumps air into the air storage tanks and is connected to the engine through gears or a v-belt.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 5, Air Brakes, 5.1.1 Air Compressor

question: At approximately what pressure does the governor stop the air compressor from pumping air (the "cut-out" level)?
choice_a: Around 150 psi
choice_b: Around 60 psi
choice_c: Around 125 psi
choice_d: Around 100 psi
explanation: When air tank pressure rises to the cut-out level, around 125 psi, the governor stops the compressor from pumping air.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 5, Air Brakes, 5.1.2 Air Compressor Governor

question: At approximately what pressure does the governor allow the compressor to start pumping again (the "cut-in" level)?
choice_a: Around 125 psi
choice_b: Around 100 psi
choice_c: Around 150 psi
choice_d: Around 55 psi
explanation: When tank pressure falls to the cut-in pressure, around 100 psi, the governor allows the compressor to start pumping again.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 5, Air Brakes, 5.1.2 Air Compressor Governor

question: What is the purpose of air storage tanks (reservoirs) in an air brake system?
choice_a: To cool the compressed air before it reaches the brake chambers
choice_b: To store alcohol for the evaporator only
choice_c: To hold compressed air, enough for several brake applications even if the compressor stops working
choice_d: To measure vehicle speed
explanation: Air storage tanks hold compressed air and will hold enough to allow the brakes to be used several times, even if the compressor stops working.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 5, Air Brakes, 5.1.3 Air Storage Tanks

question: Why is it important to drain water and oil from air tanks?
choice_a: It increases the governor cut-out pressure
choice_b: Water can freeze in cold weather and cause brake failure
choice_c: It is only a cosmetic maintenance step
choice_d: It improves fuel economy
explanation: Compressed air usually contains water and compressor oil, which are bad for the air brake system; the water can freeze in cold weather and cause brake failure.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 5, Air Brakes, 5.1.4 Air Tank Drains

question: What are the two types of air tank drain valves described in the manual?
choice_a: Primary and secondary only
choice_b: High-pressure and low-pressure
choice_c: Electric and hydraulic
choice_d: Manually operated (quarter turn or pull cable) and automatic
explanation: Each air tank drain valve is either manually operated, by turning a quarter turn or pulling a cable, or automatic, where water and oil are expelled automatically.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 5, Air Brakes, 5.1.4 Air Tank Drains

question: What is the purpose of an alcohol evaporator in some air brake systems?
choice_a: To lubricate the s-cam
choice_b: To clean the brake linings
choice_c: To put alcohol into the air system to reduce the risk of ice in valves and other parts during cold weather
choice_d: To cool the compressor
explanation: The alcohol evaporator puts alcohol into the air system to help reduce the risk of ice forming in air brake valves and other parts during cold weather.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 5, Air Brakes, 5.1.5 Alcohol Evaporator

question: At approximately what pressure is the safety relief valve, installed in the first tank the compressor pumps air to, usually set to open?
choice_a: 125 psi
choice_b: 150 psi
choice_c: 175 psi
choice_d: 100 psi
explanation: The safety valve is usually set to open at 150 psi to protect the tank and the rest of the system from too much pressure.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 5, Air Brakes, 5.1.6 Safety Valve

question: If the safety relief valve releases air, what does this indicate?
choice_a: The system is functioning exactly as intended under normal conditions
choice_b: The alcohol evaporator needs refilling
choice_c: Something is wrong and the fault should be fixed by a mechanic
choice_d: The parking brake has been engaged
explanation: If the safety valve releases air, something is wrong, and the fault should be fixed by a mechanic.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 5, Air Brakes, 5.1.6 Safety Valve

question: What can happen if a driver presses and releases the brake pedal unnecessarily and repeatedly?
choice_a: Air can be let out of the system faster than the compressor can replace it, and if pressure gets too low, the brakes won't work
choice_b: The alcohol evaporator will overflow
choice_c: The governor will permanently shut off
choice_d: It has no effect on air pressure
explanation: Pressing and releasing the pedal unnecessarily can let air out faster than the compressor can replace it, and if pressure gets too low the brakes won't work.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 5, Air Brakes, 5.1.7 The Brake Pedal

question: What is the most common type of foundation brake used at each wheel?
choice_a: The hydraulic drum brake
choice_b: The disc brake
choice_c: The s-cam drum brake
choice_d: The wedge brake
explanation: Foundation brakes are used at each wheel, and the most common type is the s-cam drum brake.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 5, Air Brakes, 5.1.8 Foundation Brakes

question: In an s-cam brake, what happens when the brake pedal is pushed?
choice_a: A hydraulic wedge directly clamps the drum
choice_b: A spring immediately releases the brake shoes
choice_c: The power screw directly rotates the wheel hub
choice_d: Air enters the brake chamber, pushing a rod that moves the slack adjuster and twists the camshaft, turning the s-cam to force the shoes against the drum
explanation: When the brake pedal is pushed, air enters each brake chamber, pushing the rod out to move the slack adjuster, which twists the brake camshaft and turns the s-cam, forcing the brake shoes against the inside of the drum.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 5, Air Brakes, 5.1.8 Foundation Brakes

question: What does it mean if the application pressure gauge shows you need increasing pressure to hold the same speed?
choice_a: The alcohol evaporator is empty
choice_b: The brakes are fading, and you should slow down and use a lower gear
choice_c: The governor cut-in pressure has increased
choice_d: This is a normal condition requiring no action
explanation: Increasing application pressure to hold the same speed means the brakes are fading, and the driver should slow down and use a lower gear; this can also be caused by brakes out of adjustment, air leaks, or mechanical problems.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 5, Air Brakes, 5.1.10 Application Pressure Gauge

question: A visible low air pressure warning signal must come on before the air pressure in the tanks falls below what level (on most vehicles)?
choice_a: 100 psi
choice_b: 75 psi
choice_c: 35 psi
choice_d: 55 psi
explanation: A warning signal you can see must come on before the air pressure in the tanks falls below 55 psi (or one half the compressor governor cutout pressure on older vehicles).
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 5, Air Brakes, 5.1.11 Low Air Pressure Warning

question: What is a "wig wag" warning device?
choice_a: A red light that only activates when the parking brake is set
choice_b: An audible alarm tied to the governor cut-out pressure
choice_c: A gauge needle that changes color
choice_d: A device that drops a mechanical arm into view when air pressure drops below 55 psi
explanation: A wig wag device drops a mechanical arm into the driver's view when pressure in the system drops below 55 psi; an automatic wig wag rises out of view when pressure rises above 55 psi.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 5, Air Brakes, 5.1.11 Low Air Pressure Warning

question: How does the air brake system turn on the brake lights when the driver applies the brakes?
choice_a: Brake lights are unrelated to the air brake system
choice_b: Through an electric switch that works by air pressure
choice_c: Through the ABS malfunction lamp circuit
choice_d: Through a mechanical linkage to the brake pedal only
explanation: The air brake system uses an electric switch that works by air pressure to turn on the brake lights when the driver applies the air brakes.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 5, Air Brakes, 5.1.12 Stop Light Switch

question: On older vehicles (made before 1975) equipped with a front brake limiting valve, what happens when the control is set to "slippery"?
choice_a: It activates the alcohol evaporator
choice_b: The limiting valve cuts the normal air pressure to the front brakes by half, actually reducing stopping power
choice_c: It doubles the pressure to the front brakes for better traction
choice_d: It disables the rear brakes entirely
explanation: In the "slippery" position, the limiting valve cuts the normal air pressure to the front brakes by half; however, this actually reduces stopping power, and front wheel skids are unlikely even on ice, so the control should be kept in "normal."
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 5, Air Brakes, 5.1.13 Front Brake Limiting Valve

question: How do spring brakes hold the vehicle's emergency and parking brakes on, given that air pressure can eventually leak away?
choice_a: By a secondary hydraulic circuit
choice_b: By mechanical force from powerful springs that are held back by air pressure while driving
choice_c: By an electric solenoid
choice_d: By the alcohol evaporator system
explanation: All trucks, truck tractors, and buses must have emergency and parking brakes held on by mechanical force, since air pressure can eventually leak away; spring brakes use powerful springs held back by air pressure while driving.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 5, Air Brakes, 5.1.14 Spring Brakes

question: In what pressure range will tractor and straight truck spring brakes come fully on?
choice_a: 55 to 75 psi
choice_b: 5 to 15 psi
choice_c: 80 to 100 psi
choice_d: 20 to 45 psi (typically 20 to 30 psi)
explanation: Tractor and straight truck spring brakes will come fully on when air pressure drops to a range of 20 to 45 psi, typically 20 to 30 psi.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 5, Air Brakes, 5.1.14 Spring Brakes

question: On newer vehicles with air brakes, what does the diamond-shaped, yellow, push-pull parking brake control knob do?
choice_a: Pulling it out releases the spring brakes; pushing it in applies them
choice_b: Pulling it out applies the parking (spring) brakes; pushing it in releases them
choice_c: It only controls the alcohol evaporator
choice_d: It adjusts the governor cut-in pressure
explanation: You pull the diamond-shaped, yellow, push-pull control knob out to put the parking brakes (spring brakes) on, and push it in to release them.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 5, Air Brakes, 5.1.15 Parking Brake Controls

question: Why should a driver never push the brake pedal down when the spring brakes are on?
choice_a: It causes the alcohol evaporator to overflow
choice_b: The brakes could be damaged by the combined forces of the springs and the air pressure
choice_c: It will disable the ABS system permanently
choice_d: It has no negative effect on any system
explanation: Pushing the brake pedal down while spring brakes are on could damage the brakes from the combined forces of the springs and air pressure, so drivers should develop the habit of not doing so.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 5, Air Brakes, 5.1.15 Parking Brake Controls

question: Truck tractors with air brakes built on or after what date are required to have antilock brakes?
choice_a: March 1, 1997
choice_b: March 1, 1998
choice_c: March 1, 1994
choice_d: March 1, 2000
explanation: Truck tractors with air brakes built on or after March 1, 1997 are required to be equipped with antilock brakes.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 5, Air Brakes, 5.1.16 Antilock Braking Systems (ABS)

question: Other air brake vehicles (trucks, buses, trailers, and converter dollies) built on or after what date are required to be equipped with ABS?
choice_a: January 1, 1999
choice_b: March 1, 1998
choice_c: March 1, 1997
choice_d: March 1, 1994
explanation: Trucks, buses, trailers, and converter dollies built on or after March 1, 1998 are required to be equipped with antilock brakes.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 5, Air Brakes, 5.1.16 Antilock Braking Systems (ABS)

question: What does ABS do to a vehicle's normal braking capability?
choice_a: ABS always increases the vehicle's total stopping power
choice_b: ABS decreases stopping power in all conditions
choice_c: ABS replaces the need for foundation brakes entirely
choice_d: ABS is an addition to normal brakes and does not decrease or increase normal braking capability; it only activates when wheels are about to lock up
explanation: ABS is an addition to your normal brakes; it does not decrease or increase your normal braking capability, and only activates when wheels are about to lock up.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 5, Air Brakes, 5.1.16 Antilock Braking Systems (ABS)

question: Does ABS necessarily shorten a vehicle's stopping distance?
choice_a: No, but it helps the driver keep the vehicle under control during hard braking
choice_b: Yes, ABS always cuts stopping distance in half
choice_c: Yes, but only on dry pavement
choice_d: ABS has no effect on control or stopping distance
explanation: ABS does not necessarily shorten your stopping distance, but it does help you keep the vehicle under control during hard braking.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 5, Air Brakes, 5.1.16 Antilock Braking Systems (ABS)

question: What is a dual air brake system?
choice_a: Two separate parking brake knobs
choice_b: A backup hydraulic system that engages if air pressure fails
choice_c: A system with two brake pedals for driver and co-driver
choice_d: Two separate air brake systems that use a single set of brake controls, each with its own air tanks, hoses, and lines
explanation: A dual air brake system has two separate air brake systems, which use a single set of brake controls; each system has its own air tanks, hoses, lines, etc.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 5, Air Brakes, 5.2 Dual Air Brake

question: Before driving a vehicle with a dual air system, how much minimum pressure should be built up in both the primary and secondary systems?
choice_a: 60 psi
choice_b: 100 psi
choice_c: 125 psi
choice_d: 150 psi
explanation: Before driving a vehicle with a dual air system, allow time for the air compressor to build up a minimum of 100 psi pressure in both the primary and secondary systems.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 5, Air Brakes, 5.2 Dual Air Brake

question: In a dual air brake system, the low air pressure warning light and buzzer should come on before pressure drops below what value in either system?
choice_a: 100 psi
choice_b: 60 psi
choice_c: 30 psi
choice_d: 45 psi
explanation: The warning light and buzzer should come on before the air pressure drops below 60 psi in either system; this value must be greater than 60 psi per manufacturer specification.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 5, Air Brakes, 5.2 Dual Air Brake

question: What should a driver do if the low air pressure warning comes on while driving a dual air brake system vehicle?
choice_a: Increase speed to reach the nearest exit quickly
choice_b: Stop right away and safely park the vehicle, then have the air brake system fixed
choice_c: Continue driving normally since a backup system will engage
choice_d: Switch the front brake limiting valve to "slippery"
explanation: If the warning comes on while driving, you should stop right away and safely park the vehicle, since one air system being low on pressure means the front or rear brakes will not be operating fully, increasing stopping distance.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 5, Air Brakes, 5.2 Dual Air Brake

question: When checking slack adjusters on s-cam brakes during the walkaround inspection, how much movement at the point where the push rod attaches likely indicates the adjuster needs adjustment?
choice_a: More than about one inch
choice_b: More than six inches
choice_c: Movement is not a valid test method
choice_d: Any movement at all, even a fraction of an inch
explanation: After parking on level ground, chocking the wheels, and releasing the parking brakes, if a slack adjuster moves more than about one inch where the push rod attaches to it, it probably needs adjustment.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 5, Air Brakes, 5.3.2 During Step 5 Walkaround Inspection

question: All vehicles built since what year have automatic slack adjusters?
explanation: The manual states that all vehicles built since 1994 have automatic slack adjusters, though they must still be checked even though they adjust themselves during full brake applications.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 5, Air Brakes, 5.3.2 During Step 5 Walkaround Inspection

question: Why is manually adjusting an automatic slack adjuster considered dangerous, according to the manual?
choice_a: It is illegal in all circumstances with no exceptions
choice_b: It generally masks an underlying mechanical problem rather than fixing it, giving a false sense of security about the brakes' effectiveness
choice_c: It has no real downside and is recommended as routine maintenance
choice_d: It voids the vehicle's warranty
explanation: The manual explains that manually adjusting an automatic slack adjuster is generally masking a mechanical problem rather than fixing it, and this is dangerous because it may give the driver a false sense of security regarding the brakes' effectiveness.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 5, Air Brakes, 5.3.2 During Step 5 Walkaround Inspection

question: During the final air brake check, the low air pressure warning signal must come on before the pressure drops below what level in the tank (or lowest-pressure tank in dual systems)?
choice_a: 55 psi
choice_b: 100 psi
choice_c: 45 psi
choice_d: 125 psi
explanation: The manual states the low air pressure warning signal must come on before the pressure drops to less than 55 psi in the air tank, or the tank with the lowest pressure in dual air systems.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 5, Air Brakes, 5.3.3 Step 7 Final Air Brake Check

question: During the final air brake check, at what pressure range should the parking brake valve pop out, causing the spring brakes to come on, as air pressure is fanned down?
choice_b: 20-45 psi (manufacturer's specification)
choice_c: 5-15 psi
explanation: As air pressure is fanned off, the parking brake valve should close (pop out) when the air pressure falls to the manufacturer's specification, in the 20 to 45 psi range, causing the spring brakes to come on.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 5, Air Brakes, 5.3.3 Step 7 Final Air Brake Check

question: In a dual air system with the engine at operating rpm, air pressure should build from 85 to 100 psi within how many seconds?
choice_a: 90 seconds
choice_b: 45 seconds
choice_c: 10 seconds
choice_d: 3 minutes
explanation: When the engine is at operating rpm, pressure should build from 85 to 100 psi within 45 seconds in dual air systems (longer buildup times can still be safe with larger than minimum tanks, per manufacturer specs).
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 5, Air Brakes, 5.3.3 Step 7 Final Air Brake Check

question: When testing air leakage rate on a fully-charged single vehicle (engine off, parking brake released), what is the maximum acceptable loss rate?
choice_a: Less than five psi in one minute
choice_b: Zero psi loss is required
choice_c: Less than ten psi in one minute
choice_d: Less than two psi in one minute
explanation: With a fully-charged air system, engine off, and parking brake released, the loss rate should be less than two psi in one minute for single vehicles (less than three psi per minute for combination vehicles).
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 5, Air Brakes, 5.3.3 Step 7 Final Air Brake Check

question: After applying 90 psi or more with the brake pedal, what is the maximum acceptable air pressure loss rate for a combination vehicle?
choice_a: No more than four psi in one minute
choice_b: No air loss is acceptable at all
choice_c: No more than ten psi in one minute
choice_d: No more than two psi in one minute
explanation: After the initial pressure drop with brakes applied, if the air pressure falls more than three psi per minute for single vehicles (more than four psi per minute for combination vehicles), the air loss rate is too much.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 5, Air Brakes, 5.3.3 Step 7 Final Air Brake Check

question: How should a driver test the parking brake during the final air brake check?
choice_a: Stop the vehicle, put the parking brake on, and gently pull against it in a low gear
choice_b: Test only visually without moving the vehicle
choice_c: Have a mechanic test it remotely
choice_d: Drive at highway speed and apply the parking brake suddenly
explanation: To test the parking brake, stop the vehicle, put the parking brake on, and gently pull against it in a low gear to confirm it will hold.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 5, Air Brakes, 5.3.3 Step 7 Final Air Brake Check

question: When driving a tractor-trailer combination equipped with ABS, how should a driver brake?
choice_a: Pump the brakes rapidly at all times
choice_b: The same way as always, using only the braking force necessary to stop safely and stay in control
choice_c: Always fully apply the brakes immediately regardless of the situation
choice_d: Brake differently depending on whether ABS is on the tractor or trailer
explanation: When driving a tractor-trailer combination with ABS, the driver should brake as always: use only the braking force necessary to stop safely and stay in control, braking the same way regardless of where the ABS is installed.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 5, Air Brakes, 5.4.2 Braking with Antilock Brakes

question: When only the tractor has ABS (not the trailer), what should a driver watch for while braking hard?
choice_a: Apply maximum brake force regardless of trailer behavior
choice_b: There is no need to watch the trailer since ABS controls it automatically
choice_c: The trailer cannot swing out under any circumstances
choice_d: Keep an eye on the trailer and let up on the brakes, if safe, if it begins to swing out
explanation: When only the tractor has ABS, the driver should maintain steering control with less chance of jackknifing, but should watch the trailer and let up on the brakes, if safe, if it begins to swing out.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 5, Air Brakes, 5.4.2 Braking with Antilock Brakes

question: What is the one exception the manual gives to normal ABS braking technique?
choice_a: If you always drive a straight truck or combination with working ABS on all axles, you can fully apply the brakes in an emergency stop
choice_b: There are no exceptions to normal braking technique
choice_c: You should always brake harder if only the trailer has ABS
choice_d: ABS should never be fully applied under any circumstance
explanation: The manual notes one exception: if you always drive a straight truck or combination with working ABS on all axles, you can fully apply the brakes in an emergency stop.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 5, Air Brakes, 5.4.2 Braking with Antilock Brakes

question: What two methods does the manual describe for braking in an emergency stop?
choice_a: Engine braking and spring braking
choice_b: Front-only braking and rear-only braking
choice_c: ABS braking and manual braking
choice_d: Controlled braking and stab braking
explanation: In an emergency stop, a driver can use either the controlled braking method or the stab braking method.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 5, Air Brakes, 5.4.3 Emergency Stops

question: In the controlled braking method, how hard should the brakes be applied?
choice_a: As hard as possible without locking the wheels, with small steering wheel movements
choice_b: Only lightly, using engine braking primarily
choice_c: In short, rapid taps regardless of wheel behavior
choice_d: All the way, then immediately release regardless of wheel lock
explanation: With controlled braking, the driver applies the brakes as hard as possible without locking the wheels, keeping steering wheel movements very small.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 5, Air Brakes, 5.4.3 Emergency Stops

question: In the stab braking method, when should the driver release the brakes?
choice_a: The brakes should never be released once applied
choice_b: Every two seconds regardless of wheel behavior
choice_c: When the wheels lock up, then reapply fully once the wheels start rolling again
choice_d: Only when the vehicle has come to a complete stop
explanation: In stab braking, the driver applies the brakes fully, releases when the wheels lock up, and reapplies the brakes fully as soon as the wheels start rolling again (it can take up to one second for wheels to start rolling after release).
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 5, Air Brakes, 5.4.3 Emergency Stops

question: What four factors make up total stopping distance for a vehicle with air brakes?
choice_a: Perception distance, reaction distance, and braking distance only
choice_b: Compressor lag, governor lag, valve lag, and shoe lag
choice_c: Weight, speed, road surface, and tire tread depth
choice_d: Perception distance, reaction distance, brake lag distance, and braking distance
explanation: The total stopping distance for a vehicle with air brakes equals perception distance plus reaction distance plus brake lag distance plus braking distance.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 5, Air Brakes, 5.4.4 Stopping Distance

question: At 55 mph on dry pavement, approximately how much distance does air brake lag add to the total stopping distance?
choice_a: About 100 feet
choice_b: About 5 feet
choice_c: About 450 feet
choice_d: About 32 feet
explanation: The air brake lag distance at 55 mph on dry pavement adds about 32 feet; total stopping distance at that speed for an average driver under good conditions is over 450 feet.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 5, Air Brakes, 5.4.4 Stopping Distance

question: What causes brake fade in an air brake system?
choice_a: Too much alcohol in the evaporator
choice_b: Excessive heat causing chemical changes in the brake lining that reduce friction, and expansion of the brake drums
choice_c: The governor cutting in too early
choice_d: Cold weather causing the air lines to contract
explanation: Brake fade results from excessive heat causing chemical changes in the brake lining, which reduce friction, and also causing expansion of the brake drums, so the shoes and linings must move farther and with reduced force.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 5, Air Brakes, 5.4.5 Brake Fading or Failure

question: How can brakes being out of adjustment contribute to overall brake fade or failure?
choice_a: Out-of-adjustment brakes have no effect on overall braking performance
choice_b: Out-of-adjustment brakes only affect fuel economy
choice_c: Out-of-adjustment brakes automatically trigger the ABS malfunction lamp
choice_d: Out-of-adjustment brakes stop doing their share of the work sooner, causing the remaining brakes to overheat and fade from carrying extra load
explanation: Brakes out of adjustment stop doing their share of the work before those that are in adjustment, causing the other brakes to overheat and fade, leaving insufficient braking to control the vehicle.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 5, Air Brakes, 5.4.5 Brake Fading or Failure

question: On a long or steep downgrade, the manual says the use of brakes should serve what role relative to engine braking?
choice_a: The brakes should do all the work while the engine is placed in neutral
choice_b: The brakes are only a supplement to the braking effect of the engine
choice_c: Engine braking should never be used on air brake vehicles
choice_d: Brakes and engine braking should never be combined
explanation: The manual states that the use of brakes on a long and/or steep downgrade is only a supplement to the braking effect of the engine.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 5, Air Brakes, 5.4.6 Proper Braking Technique

question: Using the proper downgrade braking technique, at approximately what speed below your "safe" speed should you release the brakes after applying them?
choice_a: About five mph below your safe speed
choice_b: About fifteen mph below your safe speed
choice_c: Exactly at your safe speed, never below it
choice_d: You should never release the brakes until reaching the bottom
explanation: The proper technique is to apply the brakes hard enough to feel a definite slowdown, and when speed has been reduced to approximately five mph below your safe speed, release the brakes; this application should last about three seconds.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 5, Air Brakes, 5.4.6 Proper Braking Technique

question: Why can a heavily loaded vehicle take a long distance to stop once the spring brakes engage due to low air pressure?
choice_a: Because the ABS disengages automatically at low pressure
choice_b: Because spring brakes only work on lightly loaded vehicles
choice_c: Because the spring brakes do not work on all axles
choice_d: Because the governor shuts off the engine at low pressure
explanation: A heavily loaded vehicle will take a long distance to stop when the spring brakes come on because the spring brakes do not work on all axles.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 5, Air Brakes, 5.4.7 Low Air Pressure

question: Why is it safer to stop while there is still enough air in the tanks to use the foot brakes, rather than waiting for the spring brakes to engage?
choice_a: There is no safety difference between the two
choice_b: Foot brakes cannot be used once the low air warning activates
choice_c: Controlled braking is only possible while enough air remains, and lightly loaded vehicles or those on slippery roads may skid out of control when spring brakes come on
choice_d: The spring brakes provide smoother stops than the foot brakes in every situation
explanation: Controlled braking is possible only while enough air remains in the tanks; lightly loaded vehicles or vehicles on slippery roads may skid out of control when the spring brakes come on, so it is much safer to stop using the foot brakes first.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 5, Air Brakes, 5.4.7 Low Air Pressure

question: When should a driver avoid using the parking brakes, according to the manual?
choice_a: Only during daytime hours
choice_b: The parking brakes should be used in every parking situation with no exceptions
choice_c: Whenever the vehicle is parked on flat ground
choice_d: If the brakes are very hot from a steep grade, or very wet in freezing temperatures
explanation: The manual advises not using the parking brakes if they are very hot from just coming down a steep grade, or if they are very wet in freezing temperatures, since heat can damage them and freezing moisture can lock the vehicle in place.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 5, Air Brakes, 5.4.8 Parking Brakes

question: If parking brakes cannot be used because they are too hot or too wet in freezing conditions, what should the driver do instead to secure the vehicle?
choice_a: Rely on the ABS malfunction lamp to hold the vehicle
choice_b: Use wheel chocks on a level surface
choice_c: Nothing additional is needed
choice_d: Leave the vehicle in gear with the engine running
explanation: The manual instructs using wheel chocks on a level surface to hold the vehicle when the parking brakes cannot safely be used due to heat or freezing moisture.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 5, Air Brakes, 5.4.8 Parking Brakes

question: What should a driver never do when leaving a vehicle unattended, according to the manual?
choice_a: Leave it without applying the parking brakes or chocking the wheels
choice_b: Leave the low air pressure warning light on
choice_c: Leave the engine running
choice_d: Leave the windows open
explanation: The manual warns to never leave your vehicle unattended without applying the parking brakes or chocking the wheels, since it might roll away and cause injury and damage.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 5, Air Brakes, 5.4.8 Parking Brakes

question: What does the service brake system do?
choice_a: Only functions during a total system failure
choice_b: Applies and releases the brakes when you use the brake pedal during normal driving
choice_c: Controls the ABS malfunction lamp
choice_d: Applies and releases the brakes when you use the parking brake control
explanation: The service brake system applies and releases the brakes when the driver uses the brake pedal during normal driving.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Introduction

question: During the engine compartment check on a vehicle with a belt-driven air compressor, what should be inspected?
choice_a: The ABS electronic control unit
choice_b: Only the compressor's oil color
choice_c: The alcohol evaporator wiring only
choice_d: The condition and tightness of the compressor drive belt
explanation: During Step 2 engine compartment checks, if the air compressor is belt-driven, the driver should check the condition and tightness of the belt to confirm it is in good condition.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 5, Air Brakes, 5.3.1 During Step 2 Engine Compartment Checks
